newsitem.title: USA: Dow Jones results fail to placate critics.
newsitem.headline: Dow Jones results fail to placate critics.

text.p: Dow Jones & Co Inc on Wednesday produced first quarter results in line with market expectations, but underlined that the firm is doing better in traditional publishing than in financial information services.
The results did little to avert criticism expected to re-surface at next Wednesday's shareholder meeting of a plan to plow $650 million into financial information services.
"Dow Jones markets, formerly Telerate, performed worse than I thought it had (in the first quarter)," said James Cramer, a shareholder critic of Dow Jones.

Dow Jones reported first quarter earnings per share of $0.27 down from $0.39 a year ago, and predicted that for the year it would make $1.20 to $1.40, in line with analysts' consensus of $1.31. In 1996 Dow Jones made $1.96 per share.
"The good news is the publishing did very well, while information services were a little worse than expected," said analyst Ed Atorino of Oppenheimer & Co.
"Results overall met expectations," Atorino said.

Dow Jones has been criticised for giving miserable returns to stockholders since peaking a decade ago at $56, before the 1987 crash. By 1500 EDT/1900 GMT on Wednesday the shares stood at $40, down 3/4 on the day.

Some shareholders, including members of Dow Jones' controlling Bancroft family shareholders have lashed out at the company's plans to spend $650 million catching up with its financial information service rivals.

Cramer said he hopes three new independent Dow Jones directors, American Express chief executive (CEO) Harvey Golub, Bankers Trust Co CEO Frank Newman and Pfizer Inc CEO William Steere would steer the firm away from this idea.
"These are not guys who waste shareholder money," Cramer said. He hopes they will push for a sale of Dow Jones Markets.
"I reiterate this (a sale) is the right course of action, and management is on the wrong course of action," he told Reuters. Cramer bought a one percent stake in January.
Dissident Dow Jones shareholder Michael Price, who bought a 4.7 percent stake in January, on Wednesday said that the company should concentrate on what it does best, conventional business publishing.

Business publishing, including The Wall Street Journal and Barrons, television operations and Dow Jones Interactive Publishing group, posted operating income of $50.4 million, double 1996's first quarter.
Advertising linage at The Wall Street Journal rose 21.7 percent in the quarter from a year ago.
But operating income in financial information services, which includes Dow Jones Markets and Dow Jones Newswires, tumbled 83.8 percent to $7.5 million.
"They admit Dow Jones Markets is struggling, but they said they were about on track with new developments," Atorino said.

Atorino noted losses at WBIS+, a New York City television station, and lower newsprint mill profits which pushed equity losses in the quarter to $12.7 million compared with earnings last year of $1.7 million.

Dow Jones on Tuesday announced a technology and marketing alliance with Microsoft Corp to edge the firm into profitable areas like financial transaction systems and selling news to fund managers, the "buy-side" market.

Rival Bloomberg LP has done well in this market which is growing faster than the traditional "sell-side" market for information in big brokers' trading rooms, while Reuters Holdings Plc has done well in transaction systems.

Price told TV station CNBC, he expected Dow Jones to increase the dividend this year to around $1 per share from $0.96 for 1996, which he said will soak up 83 percent of expected earnings from 49 percent in 1996.

"(Chief Executive) Peter Kann is larger dividend in part because it helps him to justify his game plan to the family members," Price said. He added that a lower dividend would increase the share price. ((-- New York Newsrom 212 859 1610))1
